newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland Catholics step up action against marches.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland Catholics step up action against marches.

text.p: Northern Ireland Catholic nationalists on Wednesday stepped up their opposition to Protestant parades as the province endured a night of sporadic violence.

Residents of Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road were due to meet Irish government ministers as part of efforts to resist an Orange Order parade scheduled for Saturday, the high point of the annual Protestant marching season.

Gerard Rice of the Lower Ormeau Concerned Community said he wanted the Irish government to back calls for the march to be diverted from the Catholic section of the road and end a situation where Protestants march because "might is right".
Britain's Northern Ireland security minister Adam Ingram said the government was still looking at ways to resolve the Ormeau Road dilemma.
"What we are looking at is ways of trying to get accommodation between those who want to march and those who are trying to resist that march," he told BBC television.
"They have got to realise the implications of their actions."
Orange Order spokemen say they have made compromises in their demands to parade along what the call the "Queen's Highway".

Northern Ireland has seen some of the worst violence in years as nationalist areas erupted in fury following a police decision to allow the Orange Order to march along the Catholic Garvaghy Road in Portadown last Sunday.
Nationalist areas were calmer overnight, with isolated incidents of shooting and petrol bombing. But the threat of further violence remained firmly in evidence.
A radical IRA splinter group, the Irish National Liberation Army (INLA), threatened to attack members of the Orange Order if they insisted on carrying out plans to march down the Lower Ormeau Road.
"If any more Loyalist marches are forced through Nationalist communities we will move from our position of defence and retaliation," an INLA statement said.

A Catholic residents' group in Londonderry, Northern Ireland's second city, called in a statement for a huge rally to protest against the holding of a march by the Apprentice Boys, another Protestant organisation, on the same day.
The 12th of July marks the anniversary of a 1690 Protestant battle victory over an invading Catholic King and is seen by Catholics as an anachronistic display of triumphalism.

The INLA claimed responsibility for several of the shooting attacks on British troops and police which have been staged nightly since Sunday's march. Two police officers have been injured but no-one has been killed.
The statement was issued hours after masked gunmen hijacked a Belfast-bound train at the border town of Newry.

Sections of a key highway were blocked by blazing cars hijacked by angry Catholic youths and security forces were again attacked by Catholic youths but the violence appeared to ebb as political tension over the weekend parade rose.

The Foreign Minister of Ireland, Britain's partner in the search for an end to the Northern Ireland conflict, appealed to Orangemen not to insist on marching down the Lower Ormeau Road. "Our concern, of course, is that historically all of these decisions are that might is right and that is on the Orange side," Ray Burke told reporters after attending the latest round of Northern Ireland peace talks on Tuesday.

His remarks were clear criticism of Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, who was embroiled in a row over a leaked government document which said her advisers agreed weeks before the Portadown parade that it should go ahead.
